body: 3 Min Read I Am Artemis: Allison Mjoen As the supercooled propellant flowed into the core stage, and NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket roared to life, Allison Mjoen and her family watched with awe and pride. Mjoen, NASA’s operations manager for the agency’s Exploration Ground Systems program, helped shape the systems and ground operations that will one day send humans back to the Moon. Over her 20-year career at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, she supported missions across the Space Shuttle Program, the International Space Station, and now she is applying that experience to Artemis. April 1, 2026, was a bright, crystal-clear day along the Florida Space Coast. The sunlight seemed to sharpen every color along the horizon. As Mjoen and her children counted down and the crowd’s voices rose around them, the rumble of the SLS rocket intensified beneath their feet. For her children, it was the chance to see what their mom had helped make possible. For Mjoen, it was a moment she would never forget. body: 6 Min Read NASA Satellites Observe Historic 2026 El Niño This visualization compares three ocean data products, sea surface temperature anomaly, apparent visible wavelength, and sea surface height anomaly, over the same months in 2025 and 2026. Signals of El Niño in each map are highlighted with pop-up labels. Credits: NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio A phenomenon rarer than a solar eclipse and more powerful than any single storm system is unfolding this fall, and NASA is tracking it closely. El Niño is a natural climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific. NASA scientists are keeping watch as it flips trade winds, redistributes ocean heat, scrambles rain patterns, and raises sea surface height across parts of the Pacific. As of October, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has said that there’s an 83% chance that the strongest El Niño since 1950 is currently unfolding. title: Carrier heavyweight warns that helping SpaceX could come back to bite the big three
summary: SpaceX's spectrum deal isn't enough to worry this carrier heavyweight.
body: TL;DR T-Mobile’s parent company, Deutsche Telekom, is casting doubt on SpaceX’s ambitions to become the fourth major US wireless carrier. CEO Tim Höttges argues that satellite connectivity can’t replace traditional cellular networks in densely populated areas and that SpaceX faces major infrastructure challenges. Höttges also warned carriers against entering into MVNO agreements with SpaceX, arguing that such partnerships could hurt their own businesses. SpaceX’s major announcement from last week has had the big three US carriers on the defensive. For reference, the Elon Musk-founded company is aiming to become a nationwide competitor to AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon, and it has done so by striking an agreement to acquire spectrum in the 800MHz band. The development should eventually help the company offer reliable indoor coverage. However, there’s a lot that needs to be done before that ambition can come to fruition, and T-Mobile’s parent company, Deutsche Telekom, is making sure SpaceX knows that.
